claim: Acute glucose restriction (AGR) induces yeast to undergo metabolic remodeling of their mevalonate pathway that is spatially coordinated at nucleus-vacuole junctions (NVJs).
source: Here, we show that in response to acute glucose restriction (AGR) yeast undergo metabolic remodeling of their mevalonate pathway that is spatially coordinated at nucleus-vacuole junctions (NVJs).
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental observations including microscopy showing Hmg1/2 localization at NVJs during AGR, and metabolic flux measurements.

claim: The NVJ serves as a metabolic platform by selectively retaining HMG-CoA Reductases (HMGCRs).
source: The NVJ serves as a metabolic platform by selectively retaining HMG-CoA Reductases (HMGCRs), driving mevalonate pathway flux in an Upc2-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by FLIP experiments showing selective retention of Hmg1-GFP at the NVJ with halftime >100s compared to ~25s elsewhere on the NE.

claim: HMGCR retention at the NVJ drives mevalonate pathway flux in an Upc2-dependent manner.
source: The NVJ serves as a metabolic platform by selectively retaining HMG-CoA Reductases (HMGCRs), driving mevalonate pathway flux in an Upc2-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by data showing upc2Δ yeast fail to partition Hmg1-GFP at the NVJ and by metabolic flux measurements.

claim: Spatial retention of HMGCRs during AGR is dependent on NVJ tether Nvj1.
source: Both spatial retention of HMGCRs and increased mevalonate pathway flux during AGR is dependent on NVJ tether Nvj1.
evidence: Supported by microscopy showing Hmg1-GFP fails to partition at the NVJ in nvj1Δ cells during AGR.

claim: Increased mevalonate pathway flux during AGR is dependent on NVJ tether Nvj1.
source: Both spatial retention of HMGCRs and increased mevalonate pathway flux during AGR is dependent on NVJ tether Nvj1.
evidence: Supported by radiolabeling experiments showing nvj1Δ yeast accumulate HMG-CoA and have reduced downstream mevalonate pathway products.

claim: HMGCRs associate into high-molecular-weight assemblies during AGR in an Nvj1-dependent manner.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that HMGCRs associate into high-molecular-weight assemblies during AGR in an Nvj1-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by blue native PAGE analysis showing Hmg1-3HA forms HMW species (~720 kDa) during AGR that are reduced in nvj1Δ cells.

claim: Loss of Nvj1-mediated HMGCR partitioning can be bypassed by artificially multimerizing HMGCRs.
source: Loss of Nvj1-mediated HMGCR partitioning can be bypassed by artificially multimerizing HMGCRs, indicating NVJ compartmentalization enhances mevalonate pathway flux by promoting the association of HMGCRs in high molecular weight assemblies.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing Hmg1-DsRed2 (tetrameric) rescues mevalonate pathway flux defects in nvj1Δ cells.

claim: NVJ compartmentalization enhances mevalonate pathway flux by promoting the association of HMGCRs in high molecular weight assemblies.
source: Loss of Nvj1-mediated HMGCR partitioning can be bypassed by artificially multimerizing HMGCRs, indicating NVJ compartmentalization enhances mevalonate pathway flux by promoting the association of HMGCRs in high molecular weight assemblies.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of mevalonate pathway flux defects by artificial multimerization of HMGCRs in nvj1Δ cells.

claim: Loss of HMGCR compartmentalization perturbs yeast growth following glucose starvation.
source: Loss of HMGCR compartmentalization perturbs yeast growth following glucose starvation, indicating it promotes adaptive metabolic remodeling.
evidence: Supported by growth resumption experiments showing nvj1Δ yeast have delayed growth resumption after AGR.

claim: HMGCR compartmentalization promotes adaptive metabolic remodeling.
source: Loss of HMGCR compartmentalization perturbs yeast growth following glucose starvation, indicating it promotes adaptive metabolic remodeling.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of compartmentalization affects growth resumption and can be rescued by exogenous mevalonate.

claim: Endogenously GFP-tagged Hmg1 and Hmg2 localize throughout the ER network and particularly on the nuclear envelope.
source: Screening revealed that endogenously GFP-tagged HMG-CoA Reductases (HMGCR) Hmg1 and Hmg2, which localize throughout ER network and particularly on the nuclear envelope (NE), enriched at the regions where the nuclear surface was in contact with the vacuole following AGR (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1A showing Hmg1-GFP and Hmg2-GFP distribution.

claim: Hmg1 and Hmg2 enrich at regions where the nuclear surface contacts the vacuole following AGR.
source: Screening revealed that endogenously GFP-tagged HMG-CoA Reductases (HMGCR) Hmg1 and Hmg2, which localize throughout ER network and particularly on the nuclear envelope (NE), enriched at the regions where the nuclear surface was in contact with the vacuole following AGR (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1A showing enrichment at nucleus-vacuole interface.

claim: The nucleus-vacuole interface where Hmg1-GFP enriches is the NVJ.
source: This nucleus-vacuole interface was confirmed to be the NVJ as Hmg1-GFP co-localized with NVJ tether Nvj1-mRuby3 following AGR treatment for 4 hr (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by co-localization imaging showing Hmg1-GFP overlaps with Nvj1-mRuby3.

claim: Hmg1 and Hmg2 are functionally redundant in mevalonate synthesis.
source: As Hmg1 and Hmg2 are functionally redundant in mevalonate synthesis, a central metabolite that supplies diverse cellular pathways including sterol biogenesis, we chose to dissect the mechanisms underlying Hmg1 NVJ partitioning.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Hmg1 and Hmg2 function.

claim: Mevalonate is a central metabolite that supplies diverse cellular pathways including sterol biogenesis.
source: As Hmg1 and Hmg2 are functionally redundant in mevalonate synthesis, a central metabolite that supplies diverse cellular pathways including sterol biogenesis, we chose to dissect the mechanisms underlying Hmg1 NVJ partitioning.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mevalonate metabolism.

claim: NVJ tethers Nvj1 and Vac8 are required for Hmg1-GFP partitioning during AGR.
source: To investigate whether the NVJ was required for Hmg1 partitioning, we imaged Hmg1-GFP in the absence of NVJ tethers Nvj1 and Vac8 (Pan et al., 2000), and found they were required for Hmg1-GFP partitioning during AGR (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 1C showing loss of Hmg1-GFP partitioning in nvj1Δ and vac8Δ cells.

claim: Hmg1-GFP NVJ partitioning peaks after approximately 4 hours of AGR.
source: Furthermore, time-lapse imaging revealed that Hmg1-GFP NVJ partitioning peaked after ~4 hr of introducing yeast to AGR (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: Supported by time-course imaging and quantification in Figure 1D-F.

claim: During peak partitioning, Hmg1-GFP is approximately 15 times enriched at the NVJ relative to other NE regions.
source: During this period, Hmg1-GFP was ~15 times enriched at the NVJ relative to other NE regions.
evidence: Supported by quantification of Hmg1 partitioning shown in Figure 1E.

claim: AGR induces time-dependent compartmentalization of Hmg1/2 at the NVJ in a Nvj1 and Vac8 dependent manner.
source: Collectively, this suggests that AGR induces the time-dependent compartmentalization of Hmg1/2 at the NVJ in a Nvj1 and Vac8 dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: None of 20 endogenously mNeonGreen-tagged proteins involved in ergosterol biosynthesis detectably enriched at the NVJ during AGR.
source: To dissect whether other proteins along the mevalonate pathway also partition at the NVJ during AGR, we imaged 20 endogenously mNeonGreen (mNG)-tagged proteins involved in ergosterol biosynthesis under ambient and AGR stress, but surprisingly none detectably enriched at the NVJ (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 2A showing no NVJ enrichment for 20 ergosterol biosynthesis proteins.

claim: The NVJ has been proposed to function in sterol transport between the vacuole and ER network.
source: As the NVJ has also been proposed to function in sterol transport between the vacuole and ER network, we also examined whether loss of the NVJ-resident proteins Osh1 and Lam6/Ltc1, implicated in the inter-organelle trafficking of lipids and/or sterols, would impact Hmg1-GFP NVJ recruitment (Murley et al., 2015; Kvam and Goldfarb, 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Osh1 and Lam6/Ltc1 are implicated in the inter-organelle trafficking of lipids and/or sterols.
source: As the NVJ has also been proposed to function in sterol transport between the vacuole and ER network, we also examined whether loss of the NVJ-resident proteins Osh1 and Lam6/Ltc1, implicated in the inter-organelle trafficking of lipids and/or sterols, would impact Hmg1-GFP NVJ recruitment (Murley et al., 2015; Kvam and Goldfarb, 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Hmg1-GFP efficiently partitions at the NVJ following AGR in both osh1Δ and lam6/ltc1Δ yeast.
source: Hmg1-GFP efficiently partitioned at the NVJ following AGR in both osh1Δ and lam6/ltc1Δ yeast (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 2B showing Hmg1-GFP partitioning in deletion strains.

claim: Detectable Hmg1/2 NVJ enrichment is unique among enzymes involved in ergosterol metabolism.
source: Collectively, this suggests that detectable Hmg1/2 NVJ enrichment is unique among enzymes involved in ergosterol metabolism, and is therefore unlikely to constitute a 'classical' multi-enzyme metabolon.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only Hmg1/2 among 20 ergosterol biosynthesis proteins enriched at the NVJ.

claim: Hmg1/2 NVJ enrichment is unlikely to constitute a 'classical' multi-enzyme metabolon.
source: Collectively, this suggests that detectable Hmg1/2 NVJ enrichment is unique among enzymes involved in ergosterol metabolism, and is therefore unlikely to constitute a 'classical' multi-enzyme metabolon.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of co-enrichment of other mevalonate pathway enzymes at the NVJ.

claim: The non-partitioned Hmg1-GFP pool can enter the NVJ.
source: Using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), we determined that the non-partitioned Hmg1-GFP pool can enter the NVJ (Figure 3A,B); therefore, there is likely no diffusion barrier at the NVJ allowing selective entry of only specific pools of Hmg1-GFP protein.
evidence: Supported by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 3A,B demonstrating fluorescence recovery at the NVJ.

claim: There is likely no diffusion barrier at the NVJ allowing selective entry of only specific pools of Hmg1-GFP protein.
source: Using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), we determined that the non-partitioned Hmg1-GFP pool can enter the NVJ (Figure 3A,B); therefore, there is likely no diffusion barrier at the NVJ allowing selective entry of only specific pools of Hmg1-GFP protein.
evidence: This is inferred from FRAP data showing Hmg1-GFP can move into the NVJ region.

claim: The average lifetime of NVJ-partitioned Hmg1-GFP is greater than 100 seconds.
source: Fluorescence loss in photobleaching (FLIP) revealed the average lifetime of NVJ-partitioned Hmg1-GFP was >100 s, compared to only ~25 s for Hmg1-GFP along the rest of the NE (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by FLIP experiments and quantification shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The average lifetime of Hmg1-GFP along the rest of the NE is approximately 25 seconds.
source: Fluorescence loss in photobleaching (FLIP) revealed the average lifetime of NVJ-partitioned Hmg1-GFP was >100 s, compared to only ~25 s for Hmg1-GFP along the rest of the NE (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by FLIP experiments and quantification shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Calculated halftimes from FLIP may underestimate the actual halftime of NVJ-partitioned Hmg1-GFP.
source: Given that most of the Hmg1-GFP signal within the NVJ-partitioned population was not photobleached to completion, calculated halftimes may underestimate the actual halftime.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration based on incomplete photobleaching.

claim: Upon AGR, Hmg1-GFP is recruited and selectively retained at the NVJ.
source: Collectively, this indicates that upon AGR, Hmg1-GFP is recruited and selectively retained at the NVJ.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on FRAP and FLIP data.

claim: The halftime of Hmg1-GFP is significantly increased during AGR in nvj1Δ cells.
source: Surprisingly, the halftime of Hmg1-GFP was also significantly increased during AGR in nvj1Δ cells.
evidence: Supported by FLIP quantification shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The reduced mobility of Hmg1-GFP in nvj1Δ cells during AGR may be connected to a change in cytoplasmic viscosity.
source: This may be connected to a change in cytoplasmic viscosity which has been examined previously (Joyner et al., 2016); however, further analysis is required to determine if this reduced mobility is specific to Hmg1-GFP or a general consequence of AGR.
evidence: This is speculation based on cited previous work on cytoplasmic viscosity changes.

claim: The integral transmembrane region of Hmg1 is sufficient for NVJ recruitment.
source: This Hmg11-525-GFP truncation was sufficient to localize to the NVJ during AGR, indicating the integral membrane region of Hmg1 was sufficient for NVJ recruitment (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Supported by microscopy of Hmg11-525-GFP truncation shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The Nvj1 cytoplasmic domain is not required for Hmg1 recruitment to the NVJ.
source: A Nvj1-mNG chimera lacking its cytoplasm-exposed region and containing a vacuole-binding PX domain in place of its Vac8-binding domain (Nvj1-PX) was sufficient to tether between the nucleus and vacuole, and was sufficient to partition Hmg1-mRuby3 at the NVJ during AGR, indicating the Nvj1 cytoplasmic domain is not required for Hmg1 recruitment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy of Nvj1-PX chimera shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Nvj1 TM region is not required for Hmg1-mRuby3 recruitment to the NVJ.
source: Similarly, a Nvj1-mNG chimera with its TM region replaced with the TM of Nvj2 (Nvj1Nvj2TM) also partitioned Hmg1-mRuby3 at the NVJ, indicating the TM and cytoplasmic regions are not required for Hmg1-mRuby3 recruitment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy of Nvj1Nvj2TM chimera shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Full length Nvj1-mNG lacking residues 15-30 of its luminal region forms an NVJ contact but fails to recruit Hmg1-mRuby3.
source: However, expression of a full length Nvj1-mNG lacking residues 15–30 (Nvj1Δ15-30) of its luminal region formed an NVJ contact but failed to recruit Hmg1-mRuby3.
evidence: Supported by microscopy and quantification of Nvj1Δ15-30 shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: Re-addition of six residues to Nvj1Δ15-30 (creating Nvj1Δ15-24) rescues Hmg1-mRuby3 recruitment.
source: Re-addition of six residues to this construct (Nvj1Δ15-24) rescued Hmg1-mRuby3 recruitment.
evidence: Supported by microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: Mutation of arginine and lysine residues at positions 28/29 to alanines (Nvj1RK→AA) ablates AGR-induced recruitment of Hmg1 to the NVJ.
source: Furthermore, mutation of arginine and lysine residues at positions 28/29 to alanines (Nvj1RK→AA) also ablated AGR-induced recruitment of Hmg1 to the NVJ, suggesting residues 25–30 of the Nvj1 luminal domain play a key role in Hmg1-mRuby3 NVJ partitioning (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: Supported by microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: Residues 25-30 of the Nvj1 luminal domain play a key role in Hmg1-mRuby3 NVJ partitioning.
source: Furthermore, mutation of arginine and lysine residues at positions 28/29 to alanines (Nvj1RK→AA) also ablated AGR-induced recruitment of Hmg1 to the NVJ, suggesting residues 25–30 of the Nvj1 luminal domain play a key role in Hmg1-mRuby3 NVJ partitioning (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This is inferred from the deletion and mutation analysis of Nvj1 luminal domain.

claim: The ER embedded region of Hmg1 is recruited to the NVJ in a manner requiring the ER-luminal Nvj1 region.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that the ER embedded region of Hmg1 is recruited to the NVJ in a manner requiring the ER-luminal Nvj1 region, and that Hmg1 partitioning is not dependent on the Hmg1 cytoplasmic catalytic domain nor the Nvj1 cytoplasmic/vacuole binding region.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the truncation and chimera experiments.

claim: Hmg1 partitioning is not dependent on the Hmg1 cytoplasmic catalytic domain.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that the ER embedded region of Hmg1 is recruited to the NVJ in a manner requiring the ER-luminal Nvj1 region, and that Hmg1 partitioning is not dependent on the Hmg1 cytoplasmic catalytic domain nor the Nvj1 cytoplasmic/vacuole binding region.
evidence: Supported by data showing Hmg11-525-GFP (lacking catalytic domain) is sufficient for NVJ localization.

claim: Hmg1 partitioning is not dependent on the Nvj1 cytoplasmic/vacuole binding region.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that the ER embedded region of Hmg1 is recruited to the NVJ in a manner requiring the ER-luminal Nvj1 region, and that Hmg1 partitioning is not dependent on the Hmg1 cytoplasmic catalytic domain nor the Nvj1 cytoplasmic/vacuole binding region.
evidence: Supported by data showing Nvj1-PX chimera (lacking cytoplasmic domain) can recruit Hmg1.

claim: The NVJ was previously identified as a site for starvation-induced microautophagy of the nucleus.
source: The NVJ was previously identified as a site for starvation-induced microautophagy of the nucleus (Roberts et al., 2003), where NVJ-associated proteins accumulate and are subsequently engulfed by the vacuole.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: HMGCRs are known to undergo proteasomal degradation during specific metabolic cues.
source: HMGCRs are also known to undergo proteasomal degradation during specific metabolic cues.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about HMGCR regulation.

claim: AGR increases steady-state Hmg1-GFP protein levels.
source: AGR increased steady-state Hmg1-GFP protein levels, indicating glucose restriction promoted Hmg1 protein accumulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Glucose restriction promotes Hmg1 protein accumulation.
source: AGR increased steady-state Hmg1-GFP protein levels, indicating glucose restriction promoted Hmg1 protein accumulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the immunoblot data showing increased Hmg1-GFP levels during AGR.

claim: nvj1Δ yeast display a more marked increase in Hmg1-GFP protein compared to wildtype during AGR.
source: Interestingly, nvj1Δ yeast displayed a more marked increase in Hmg1-GFP protein compared to wildtype.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Treatment with proteasome inhibitor MG132 results in only a moderate increase in steady state Hmg1-GFP protein levels during AGR.
source: To determine the influence of proteasomal degradation on Hmg1 protein levels during AGR, we treated cells with proteasome inhibitor MG132 and observed only a moderate increase in steady state Hmg1-GFP protein levels (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Treatment with translation inhibitor cycloheximide during AGR returns Hmg1-GFP protein abundance to levels comparable with log-phase cells.
source: In contrast, treatment with the translation inhibitor cycloheximide during AGR returned Hmg1-GFP protein abundance to levels comparable with log-phase cells.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Proteasomal degradation does not contribute significantly to controlling Hmg1-GFP protein abundance during AGR.
source: Collectively, this analysis suggests that proteasomal degradation does not contribute significantly to controlling Hmg1-GFP protein abundance during AGR, and the increase is likely due to de novo protein synthesis during glucose restriction.
evidence: This is inferred from the modest effect of MG132 and the strong effect of cycloheximide on Hmg1-GFP levels.

claim: The increase in Hmg1-GFP protein during AGR is likely due to de novo protein synthesis during glucose restriction.
source: Collectively, this analysis suggests that proteasomal degradation does not contribute significantly to controlling Hmg1-GFP protein abundance during AGR, and the increase is likely due to de novo protein synthesis during glucose restriction.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of cycloheximide blocking the AGR-induced increase in Hmg1-GFP.

claim: snf1Δ yeast maintain AGR-induced Hmg1-GFP partitioning at the NVJ.
source: Surprisingly, snf1Δ yeast maintained AGR-induced Hmg1-GFP partitioning at the NVJ, indicating Hmg1-GFP recruitment to the NVJ was not dependent on Snf1/AMPK signaling (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Hmg1-GFP recruitment to the NVJ is not dependent on Snf1/AMPK signaling.
source: Surprisingly, snf1Δ yeast maintained AGR-induced Hmg1-GFP partitioning at the NVJ, indicating Hmg1-GFP recruitment to the NVJ was not dependent on Snf1/AMPK signaling (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Hmg1-GFP still partitions at the NVJ in snf1Δ cells.

claim: upc2Δ yeast fail to partition Hmg1-GFP at the NVJ during AGR.
source: Indeed upc2Δ yeast failed to partition Hmg1-GFP at the NVJ during AGR, and this was specific to upc2Δ, as Hmg1-GFP maintained NVJ partitioning in ecm22Δ yeast, a Upc2 paralog (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Supported by microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Hmg1-GFP maintains NVJ partitioning in ecm22Δ yeast.
source: Indeed upc2Δ yeast failed to partition Hmg1-GFP at the NVJ during AGR, and this was specific to upc2Δ, as Hmg1-GFP maintained NVJ partitioning in ecm22Δ yeast, a Upc2 paralog (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Supported by microscopy shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Neither Nvj1 localization, Nvj1 expression, nor NVJ size is affected in the absence of Upc2.
source: We found that neither Nvj1 localization, Nvj1 expression, nor NVJ size was affected in the absence of Upc2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C); therefore, loss of Hmg1 NVJ partitioning in upc2Δ cells occurs independently of Nvj1.
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Loss of Hmg1 NVJ partitioning in upc2Δ cells occurs independently of Nvj1.
source: We found that neither Nvj1 localization, Nvj1 expression, nor NVJ size was affected in the absence of Upc2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C); therefore, loss of Hmg1 NVJ partitioning in upc2Δ cells occurs independently of Nvj1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Nvj1 is unaffected in upc2Δ cells.

claim: There are unidentified factors needed for Hmg1 NVJ partitioning that require the presence of Upc2.
source: These data suggest that there are yet unidentified factors that are needed for Hmg1 NVJ partitioning that require the presence of Upc2, as well as the luminal region of Nvj1, and that partitioning might be uncoupled from Hmg1 protein expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the Upc2 requirement for partitioning that is independent of Nvj1 expression/localization.

claim: Hmg1 NVJ partitioning might be uncoupled from Hmg1 protein expression.
source: These data suggest that there are yet unidentified factors that are needed for Hmg1 NVJ partitioning that require the presence of Upc2, as well as the luminal region of Nvj1, and that partitioning might be uncoupled from Hmg1 protein expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Hmg1-GFP expression is unchanged in upc2Δ cells despite loss of partitioning.

claim: Hmg1-GFP NVJ partitioning is induced by treatment with the squalene epoxidase inhibitor terbinafine.
source: In line with this, Hmg1-GFP NVJ partitioning was also induced by treatment with the squalene epoxidase inhibitor terbinafine, which blocks de novo ergosterol biogenesis (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: Supported by microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 4G-I.

claim: Terbinafine blocks de novo ergosterol biogenesis.
source: In line with this, Hmg1-GFP NVJ partitioning was also induced by treatment with the squalene epoxidase inhibitor terbinafine, which blocks de novo ergosterol biogenesis (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about terbinafine's mechanism of action.

claim: Following 4 hours of AGR when Hmg1-GFP is NVJ partitioned, yeast exhibit approximately 30% more steady-state levels of sterol-esters.
source: Indeed, following 4 hr of AGR when Hmg1-GFP is NVJ partitioned, yeast exhibited ~30% more steady-state levels of sterol-esters (SE), while free ergosterol levels were unchanged (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by TLC quantification shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Free ergosterol levels are unchanged following 4 hours of AGR.
source: Indeed, following 4 hr of AGR when Hmg1-GFP is NVJ partitioned, yeast exhibited ~30% more steady-state levels of sterol-esters (SE), while free ergosterol levels were unchanged (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by TLC quantification shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Co-treatment with HMGCR inhibitor lovastatin during AGR suppresses the elevation in sterol-ester levels.
source: Co-treatment with the HMGCR inhibitor lovastatin during AGR suppressed this SE elevation, indicating the elevated SE pool originated from de novo SE synthesis rather than esterification of pre-existing ergosterol.
evidence: Supported by TLC quantification shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The elevated sterol-ester pool during AGR originates from de novo SE synthesis rather than esterification of pre-existing ergosterol.
source: Co-treatment with the HMGCR inhibitor lovastatin during AGR suppressed this SE elevation, indicating the elevated SE pool originated from de novo SE synthesis rather than esterification of pre-existing ergosterol.
evidence: This is inferred from the lovastatin suppression of SE elevation.

claim: AGR induces an Upc2-dependent compartmentalization of Hmg1 at the NVJ that correlates with elevated de novo SE synthesis.
source: Altogether, this suggests that AGR induces an Upc2-dependent compartmentalization of Hmg1 at the NVJ, which correlates with elevated de novo SE synthesis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the Upc2 requirement for partitioning and the SE elevation during AGR.

claim: nvj1Δ yeast exhibit significantly elevated 14C-labeled HMG-CoA after a 15-minute radio-pulse.
source: Indeed, nvj1Δ yeast exhibited significantly elevated 14C-labeled HMG-CoA after a 15-min radio-pulse, and contained significantly less 14C-labeled squalene, ergosterol, and SE (Figure 5C–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by radiolabeling and scintillation counting shown in Figure 5C.

claim: nvj1Δ yeast contain significantly less 14C-labeled squalene, ergosterol, and SE after a 15-minute radio-pulse.
source: Indeed, nvj1Δ yeast exhibited significantly elevated 14C-labeled HMG-CoA after a 15-min radio-pulse, and contained significantly less 14C-labeled squalene, ergosterol, and SE (Figure 5C–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by radiolabeling and quantification shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: 14C-diacylglycerol (DAG) is not significantly impacted in nvj1Δ yeast.
source: However, 14C-diacylglycerol (DAG) was not significantly impacted, suggesting these alterations were specific to mevalonate pathway flux and not due to a non-specific dilution of the 14C-acetate radiolabel in nvj1Δ cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by radiolabeling and quantification shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Alterations in mevalonate pathway flux in nvj1Δ cells are specific to the mevalonate pathway and not due to non-specific dilution of the 14C-acetate radiolabel.
source: However, 14C-diacylglycerol (DAG) was not significantly impacted, suggesting these alterations were specific to mevalonate pathway flux and not due to a non-specific dilution of the 14C-acetate radiolabel in nvj1Δ cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is inferred from the unchanged DAG levels serving as a control for general lipid metabolism.

claim: nvj1Δ yeast display slower growth in culture following an AGR to SC+glucose transition compared to wildtype.
source: Indeed, nvj1Δ yeast displayed slower growth in culture following an AGR to SC+glucose transition compared to WT (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The growth defect in nvj1Δ yeast following AGR is rescued by addition of exogenous mevalonate.
source: Notably, this was rescued by addition of exogenous mevalonate, suggesting the growth defect was attributed to defects in the mevalonate pathway (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data with mevalonate addition shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The growth defect in nvj1Δ yeast following AGR is attributed to defects in the mevalonate pathway.
source: Notably, this was rescued by addition of exogenous mevalonate, suggesting the growth defect was attributed to defects in the mevalonate pathway (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of the growth defect by exogenous mevalonate.

claim: nvj1Δ cells have a significant delay in growth resumption following an SC to SC+glucose transition.
source: Quantifying the time required for growth resumption following this SC to SC+glucose transition, as measured by the appearance of the first daughter bud, showed that nvj1Δ cells had a significant delay in growth resumption (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by single-cell time-lapse imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Nvj1RK→AA cells accumulate labeled HMG-CoA after a short pulse with 14C-acetate.
source: As seen for nvj1Δ cells, Nvj1RK→AA cells accumulated labeled HMG-CoA after a short pulse with 14C-acetate (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by radiolabeling and quantification shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 14C-labeled squalene, ergosterol, and sterol-esters are significantly decreased in the Nvj1RK→AA mutant.
source: Furthermore, 14C-labeled squalene, ergosterol, and sterol-esters were significantly decreased in the Nvj1RK→AA mutant, while DAG production was unaffected (Figure 6B–D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by radiolabeling and quantification shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: DAG production is unaffected in the Nvj1RK→AA mutant.
source: Furthermore, 14C-labeled squalene, ergosterol, and sterol-esters were significantly decreased in the Nvj1RK→AA mutant, while DAG production was unaffected (Figure 6B–D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by radiolabeling and quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nvj1RK→AA mutant cells experience growth resumption delay following an SC to SC+glucose media transition, similar to nvj1Δ cells.
source: We also observed by single-cell time lapse imaging that the Nvj1RK→AA mutant cells experience growth resumption delay following an SC to SC+glucose media transition, similar to nvj1Δ cells (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: Supported by single-cell time-lapse imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Hmg1-mRuby3 fluorescence intensity in Nvj1FL and Nvj1RK→AA cells are comparable during AGR.
source: It is unlikely that these effects can be contributed to different Hmg1 expression in the given backgrounds, as Hmg1-mRuby3 fluorescence intensity in Nvj1FL and Nvj1RK→AA cells were comparable during AGR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Hmg1 partitioning at the NVJ, and not simply the presence of an NVJ contact, contributes to increased mevalonate pathway flux.
source: Overall, this further supports a model where Hmg1 partitioning at the NVJ, and not simply the presence of an NVJ contact, contributes to increased mevalonate pathway flux and resumption of growth following glucose starvation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the Nvj1RK→AA mutant data showing NVJ formation without Hmg1 recruitment still causes defects.

claim: Hmg1 partitioning at the NVJ contributes to resumption of growth following glucose starvation.
source: Overall, this further supports a model where Hmg1 partitioning at the NVJ, and not simply the presence of an NVJ contact, contributes to increased mevalonate pathway flux and resumption of growth following glucose starvation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the growth resumption data for Nvj1RK→AA mutant.

claim: ADHpr:Hmg1-GFP yeast maintain similar Hmg1-GFP protein levels with and without AGR treatment.
source: This new strain (ADHpr:Hmg1-GFP) maintained similar Hmg1-GFP protein levels with and without AGR treatment, and in the presence or absence of Nvj1 (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: ADHpr:Hmg1-GFP yeast maintain similar Hmg1-GFP protein levels in the presence or absence of Nvj1.
source: This new strain (ADHpr:Hmg1-GFP) maintained similar Hmg1-GFP protein levels with and without AGR treatment, and in the presence or absence of Nvj1 (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: ADHpr:Hmg1-GFP yeast still partition Hmg1-GFP at the NVJ during AGR in an Nvj1-dependent manner.
source: Critically, ADHpr:Hmg1-GFP yeast still partitioned Hmg1-GFP at the NVJ during AGR in an Nvj1-dependent manner, indicating we had uncoupled Hmg1 protein levels from Hmg1-GFP spatial compartmentalization (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by microscopy shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The ADHpr:Hmg1-GFP system uncouples Hmg1 protein levels from Hmg1-GFP spatial compartmentalization.
source: Critically, ADHpr:Hmg1-GFP yeast still partitioned Hmg1-GFP at the NVJ during AGR in an Nvj1-dependent manner, indicating we had uncoupled Hmg1 protein levels from Hmg1-GFP spatial compartmentalization (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is inferred from the constant Hmg1 expression but maintained partitioning behavior.

claim: nvj1Δ yeast with ADHpr:Hmg1-GFP display exacerbated alterations in mevalonate pathway flux.
source: Radio-pulse analysis revealed that nvj1Δ yeast with ADHpr:Hmg1-GFP displayed exacerbated alterations in mevalonate pathway flux, exhibiting elevated 14C-labeled HMG-CoA levels and decreased 14C-squalene, ergosterol, and SEs (Figure 6J–M, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by radiolabeling and quantification shown in Figure 6J-M.

claim: 14C-DAG levels are unaffected in nvj1Δ yeast with ADHpr:Hmg1-GFP.
source: Once again, 14C-DAG levels were unaffected, indicating that nvj1Δ yeast manifested specific defects in mevalonate metabolism and not other ER-associated lipid metabolic pathways (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by radiolabeling and quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: nvj1Δ yeast manifest specific defects in mevalonate metabolism and not other ER-associated lipid metabolic pathways.
source: Once again, 14C-DAG levels were unaffected, indicating that nvj1Δ yeast manifested specific defects in mevalonate metabolism and not other ER-associated lipid metabolic pathways (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is inferred from the unchanged DAG levels serving as a control.

claim: Hmg1-GFP NVJ spatial partitioning, independent of Hmg1 protein levels, promotes mevalonate pathway flux.
source: This suggests that Hmg1-GFP NVJ spatial partitioning, independent of Hmg1 protein levels, promotes mevalonate pathway flux.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the ADHpr:Hmg1-GFP system showing defects despite constant Hmg1 levels.

claim: Human HMGCR requires tetramerization for catalytic activity.
source: Similarly, human HMGCR requires tetramerization for catalytic activity (Istvan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Hmg1 associates in high-molecular-weight species corresponding to an approximate molecular mass of 720 kDa.
source: Indeed, when we analyzed Hmg1-3HA using blue native PAGE (BN-PAGE) we found that Hmg1 associated in high-molecular-weight (HMW) species corresponding to an approximate molecular mass of 720 kDa (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Appearance of Hmg1 HMW species is dramatically increased during AGR.
source: Appearance of Hmg1 HMW species was dramatically increased during AGR, and HMW species were significantly reduced in nvj1Δ cells.
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE analysis and quantification shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Hmg1 HMW species are significantly reduced in nvj1Δ cells.
source: Appearance of Hmg1 HMW species was dramatically increased during AGR, and HMW species were significantly reduced in nvj1Δ cells.
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE analysis and quantification shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Differences in HMW species abundance are not simply due to Hmg1-3HA expression differences.
source: Differences in HMW species abundance was not simply due to Hmg1-3HA expression, as the trend was observed even when Hmg1-3HA loading was adjusted evenly as observed by SDS-PAGE from the same samples (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by normalized quantification accounting for total Hmg1 expression shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Artificial multimerization of Hmg1 via DsRed2 tagging in nvj1Δ cells rescues the elevated 14C-labeled HMG-CoA phenotype.
source: As expected, nvj1Δ cells tagged with mRuby3 still manifested elevated 14C-labeled HMG-CoA and reduced squalene, ergosterol, and SE labeling associated with NVJ loss (Figure 7D–G). Strikingly, these perturbations were rescued in the nvj1Δ Hmg1-DsRed2 strain, closely mirroring wildtype 14C-labeled levels of Hmg-CoA, squalene, ergosterol, and SE (Figure 7D–G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by radiolabeling and quantification shown in Figure 7D-G.

claim: Artificial multimerization of Hmg1 via DsRed2 tagging in nvj1Δ cells rescues the reduced squalene, ergosterol, and SE labeling phenotypes.
source: As expected, nvj1Δ cells tagged with mRuby3 still manifested elevated 14C-labeled HMG-CoA and reduced squalene, ergosterol, and SE labeling associated with NVJ loss (Figure 7D–G). Strikingly, these perturbations were rescued in the nvj1Δ Hmg1-DsRed2 strain, closely mirroring wildtype 14C-labeled levels of Hmg-CoA, squalene, ergosterol, and SE (Figure 7D–G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by radiolabeling and quantification shown in Figure 7D-G.

claim: Appending either mRuby3 or DsRed2 tags to Hmg1 does not significantly alter expression of the protein.
source: Once again, appending either mRuby3 or DsRed2 tags to Hmg1 did not significantly alter expression of the protein from what was observed with other tags, and our data cannot be explained by differences in Hmg1 expression alone (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Artificial multimerization of Hmg1 can bypass the loss of NVJ-mediated Hmg1 compartmentalization.
source: Collectively, this indicates that artificial multimerization of Hmg1 can bypass the loss of NVJ-mediated Hmg1 compartmentalization.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the rescue of mevalonate pathway flux defects by Hmg1-DsRed2.

claim: Expression of Hmg1-DsRed2 in nvj1Δ cells rescues the growth resumption delay.
source: As expected, growth resumption delay was observed in nvj1Δ yeast expressing Hmg1-mRuby3. Remarkably, expression of Hmg1-DsRed2 in nvj1Δ cells rescued this defect (Figure 7H,I).
evidence: Supported by single-cell time-lapse imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7H,I.

claim: NVJ-dependent Hmg1 spatial compartmentalization or artificial multimerization enhances mevalonate pathway flux.
source: Collectively, this is consistent with a model where NVJ-dependent Hmg1 spatial compartmentalization via NVJ partitioning or artificial multimerization enhances mevalonate pathway flux as well as defects in growth resumption following glucose starvation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the rescue experiments with Hmg1-DsRed2.

claim: NVJ-dependent Hmg1 spatial compartmentalization or artificial multimerization rescues defects in growth resumption following glucose starvation.
source: Collectively, this is consistent with a model where NVJ-dependent Hmg1 spatial compartmentalization via NVJ partitioning or artificial multimerization enhances mevalonate pathway flux as well as defects in growth resumption following glucose starvation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the growth resumption rescue by Hmg1-DsRed2.

claim: Acute changes in nutrient availability trigger metabolic remodeling characterized by alterations in metabolic pathway flux and metabolite supply and demand.
source: Acute changes in nutrient availability trigger metabolic remodeling that is characterized by alterations in metabolic pathway flux and metabolite supply and demand.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about metabolic responses to nutrient changes.

claim: Changes in nutrient availability can drive the subcellular re-distribution of enzymes within cells.
source: Changes in nutrient availability can drive the subcellular re-distribution of enzymes within cells, as well as the formation of enzyme assemblies or complexes that promote or fine-tune metabolic pathways.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about cellular responses to nutrient changes.

claim: Changes in nutrient availability can drive the formation of enzyme assemblies or complexes that promote or fine-tune metabolic pathways.
source: Changes in nutrient availability can drive the subcellular re-distribution of enzymes within cells, as well as the formation of enzyme assemblies or complexes that promote or fine-tune metabolic pathways.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about cellular responses to nutrient changes.

claim: AGR in yeast enhances mevalonate pathway flux.
source: Here, we present evidence that AGR in yeast enhances mevalonate pathway flux, and propose the mechanism underlying this requires the spatial compartmentalization of the rate-limiting HMGCR enzymes at the yeast NVJ (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the radiolabeling experiments showing increased mevalonate pathway products.

claim: The mechanism underlying enhanced mevalonate pathway flux during AGR requires the spatial compartmentalization of the rate-limiting HMGCR enzymes at the yeast NVJ.
source: Here, we present evidence that AGR in yeast enhances mevalonate pathway flux, and propose the mechanism underlying this requires the spatial compartmentalization of the rate-limiting HMGCR enzymes at the yeast NVJ (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is the main proposed model based on all the experimental evidence presented.

claim: Hmg1 is recruited and selectively retained at the NVJ in a manner requiring basic residues within the Nvj1 luminal domain.
source: Through time-lapse and FRAP/FLIP-based imaging, we find that Hmg1 is recruited and selectively retained at the NVJ in a manner requiring basic residues within the Nvj1 luminal domain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the FRAP/FLIP data and Nvj1 truncation experiments.

claim: Hmg1 partitioning at the NVJ can be uncoupled from Nvj1 binding of Vac8.
source: We also demonstrate that Hmg1 partitioning at the NVJ can be uncoupled from Nvj1 binding of Vac8, which further supports a model where Hmg1 partitioning is being controlled predominantly from the ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the Nvj1-PX chimera data showing Hmg1 recruitment without Vac8 binding.

claim: Hmg1 partitioning is being controlled predominantly from the ER.
source: We also demonstrate that Hmg1 partitioning at the NVJ can be uncoupled from Nvj1 binding of Vac8, which further supports a model where Hmg1 partitioning is being controlled predominantly from the ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for ER-luminal Nvj1 regions and ER-embedded Hmg1 regions.

claim: Hmg1 may be selectively recruited as an enzyme 'client' to the Nvj1 'scaffold' during AGR.
source: One model is that Hmg1 is selectively recruited as an enzyme 'client' to the Nvj1 'scaffold' during AGR, but we cannot rule out the possibility that other factors may be involved together with Nvj1 in Hmg1 selective retention at the NVJ.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the selective retention data.

claim: Other factors may be involved together with Nvj1 in Hmg1 selective retention at the NVJ.
source: One model is that Hmg1 is selectively recruited as an enzyme 'client' to the Nvj1 'scaffold' during AGR, but we cannot rule out the possibility that other factors may be involved together with Nvj1 in Hmg1 selective retention at the NVJ.
evidence: This is speculation acknowledging the possibility of additional unidentified factors.

claim: Upc2 influences Hmg1 independent of either Nvj1 expression or localization.
source: Indeed, Upc2, a sterol-sensing transcription factor required for Hmg1 NVJ partitioning, appears to influence Hmg1 independent of either Nvj1 expression or localization, which may suggest additional factors required for Hmg1 partitioning at the NVJ.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing Upc2 is required for partitioning but doesn't affect Nvj1.

claim: Additional factors may be required for Hmg1 partitioning at the NVJ beyond Nvj1 and Upc2.
source: Indeed, Upc2, a sterol-sensing transcription factor required for Hmg1 NVJ partitioning, appears to influence Hmg1 independent of either Nvj1 expression or localization, which may suggest additional factors required for Hmg1 partitioning at the NVJ.
evidence: This is speculation based on the Upc2 requirement that is independent of Nvj1.

claim: The requirement of Upc2 for Hmg1 NVJ partitioning is consistent with AGR stress producing a cellular demand for mevalonate.
source: Both the requirement of Upc2 and the sufficiency of the Erg1 inhibitor terbinafine to induce Hmg1 NVJ partitioning is consistent with AGR stress producing a cellular demand for mevalonate.
evidence: This is inferred from the role of Upc2 as a sterol-sensing transcription factor and terbinafine's effect.

claim: The sufficiency of the Erg1 inhibitor terbinafine to induce Hmg1 NVJ partitioning is consistent with AGR stress producing a cellular demand for mevalonate.
source: Both the requirement of Upc2 and the sufficiency of the Erg1 inhibitor terbinafine to induce Hmg1 NVJ partitioning is consistent with AGR stress producing a cellular demand for mevalonate.
evidence: This is inferred from terbinafine blocking ergosterol synthesis and inducing Hmg1 partitioning.

claim: An increase in de novo SE synthesis is observed during AGR.
source: In line with this, we observe an increase in de novo SE synthesis during AGR; however, we cannot rule out that other mevalonate-derived metabolites may play important roles during AGR.
evidence: Supported by TLC data showing increased SE levels during AGR.

claim: Other mevalonate-derived metabolites may play important roles during AGR.
source: In line with this, we observe an increase in de novo SE synthesis during AGR; however, we cannot rule out that other mevalonate-derived metabolites may play important roles during AGR.
evidence: This is speculation acknowledging that mevalonate feeds multiple pathways.

claim: AGR is expected to promote a metabolic switch to mitochondrial respiration.
source: In fact, we would expect AGR to promote a metabolic switch to mitochondrial respiration, which in part utilizes at least one mevalonate-derived metabolite, coenzyme Q, to function as an electron carrier.
evidence: This is inferred from general knowledge about cellular responses to glucose restriction.

claim: Mitochondrial respiration utilizes coenzyme Q, a mevalonate-derived metabolite, to function as an electron carrier.
source: In fact, we would expect AGR to promote a metabolic switch to mitochondrial respiration, which in part utilizes at least one mevalonate-derived metabolite, coenzyme Q, to function as an electron carrier.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial respiration.

claim: Steady-state SE levels do not significantly decline in nvj1Δ cells.
source: In support of this, we do not observe significant decline of steady-state SE levels in nvj1Δ cells, suggesting that mevalonate may be shunted into several pathways during AGR.
evidence: Supported by TLC data showing similar steady-state SE levels in WT and nvj1Δ cells.

claim: Mevalonate may be shunted into several pathways during AGR.
source: In support of this, we do not observe significant decline of steady-state SE levels in nvj1Δ cells, suggesting that mevalonate may be shunted into several pathways during AGR.
evidence: This is inferred from the maintained SE levels despite reduced flux through the mevalonate pathway.

claim: Mevalonate pathway flux during AGR is tightly correlated with the ability to form HMW Hmg1 species at the NVJ.
source: Thus, mevalonate pathway flux during AGR appears tightly correlated with the ability to form HMW Hmg1 species at the NVJ, rather than the total Hmg1 protein level in the cell.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the BN-PAGE data and rescue by artificial multimerization.

claim: Mevalonate pathway flux during AGR is not primarily determined by the total Hmg1 protein level in the cell.
source: Thus, mevalonate pathway flux during AGR appears tightly correlated with the ability to form HMW Hmg1 species at the NVJ, rather than the total Hmg1 protein level in the cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the ADHpr:Hmg1-GFP data showing defects despite constant Hmg1 levels.

claim: AGR-induced metabolic remodeling of mevalonate metabolism is spatially coordinated at the NVJ via selective retention of HMGCRs and their subsequent incorporation into HMW species.
source: Collectively, we present a model where AGR-induced metabolic remodeling of mevalonate metabolism is spatially coordinated at the NVJ via selective retention of HMGCRs and their subsequent incorporation into HMW species.
evidence: This is the main proposed model summarizing all the experimental findings.

claim: Inter-organelle contact sites may act as platforms that slow the diffusion of proteins that enter them via their interactions with resident tether 'scaffolds'.
source: An intriguing possibility is that, in general, inter-organelle contact sites act as platforms that slow the diffusion of proteins that enter them via their interactions with resident tether 'scaffolds', thus increasing the local concentrations of proteins and enzymes sufficient to fine-tune metabolic flux.
evidence: This is speculation about a general mechanism based on the findings with Hmg1 at the NVJ.

claim: Slowing protein diffusion at inter-organelle contact sites may increase local concentrations of proteins and enzymes sufficient to fine-tune metabolic flux.
source: An intriguing possibility is that, in general, inter-organelle contact sites act as platforms that slow the diffusion of proteins that enter them via their interactions with resident tether 'scaffolds', thus increasing the local concentrations of proteins and enzymes sufficient to fine-tune metabolic flux.
evidence: This is speculation about a general mechanism based on the selective retention data.

claim: Glucose and other nutrient limitations can induce autophagy.
source: Glucose and other nutrient limitations can induce autophagy and have previously been shown to induce micro-lipophagy, where lipid droplets are engulfed by the yeast vacuole (Seo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Nutrient limitations have been shown to induce micro-lipophagy, where lipid droplets are engulfed by the yeast vacuole.
source: Glucose and other nutrient limitations can induce autophagy and have previously been shown to induce micro-lipophagy, where lipid droplets are engulfed by the yeast vacuole (Seo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: LDs accumulate in close proximity to the NVJ during periods of glucose limitation.
source: Indeed, we have observed that LDs accumulate in close proximity to the NVJ during periods of glucose limitation (Hariri et al., 2018; Hariri et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: The relationship between LD biogenesis and HMGCR partitioning at the NVJ is not fully resolved and requires further study.
source: The relationship between LD biogenesis and HMGCR partitioning at the NVJ is not fully resolved here and requires further study.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current study.

claim: The spatial re-organization of HMGCRs may contribute to LD biogenesis or compositional remodeling during the general metabolic remodeling required during glucose restriction.
source: An intriguing possibility is that the spatial re-organization of HMGCRs may contribute to LD biogenesis or compositional remodeling during the general metabolic remodeling required during glucose restriction.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible connection between HMGCR partitioning and LD biology.

claim: Yeast glucose starvation induces the formation of several cytoplasmic enzyme assemblies involved in nucleotide (Ura7), amino acid (Gly1), and lipid (Acs1) metabolism.
source: In addition to inducing the compartmentalization of HMGCRs at the NVJ, yeast glucose starvation has also been shown to induce the formation of several cytoplasmic enzyme assemblies involved in nucleotide (Ura7), amino acid (Gly1), and lipid (Acs1) metabolism (Munder et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Cytoplasmic enzyme assemblies formed during glucose starvation are thought to reduce enzymatic activity and promote the transition into cellular dormancy.
source: These cytoplasmic assemblies are thought to reduce enzymatic activity and promote the transition into cellular dormancy.
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the function of these assemblies.

claim: In the liver, the protein Mig12 binds to cytosolic acetyl-CoA carboxylases (Acc) and promotes their polymerization and catalytic activity.
source: In the liver, the protein Mig12 binds to cytosolic acetyl-CoA carboxylases (Acc) and promotes their polymerization and catalytic activity, which elevates fatty acid synthesis and eventual triglyceride accumulation in hepatocytes (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Mig12-promoted polymerization of Acc elevates fatty acid synthesis and eventual triglyceride accumulation in hepatocytes.
source: In the liver, the protein Mig12 binds to cytosolic acetyl-CoA carboxylases (Acc) and promotes their polymerization and catalytic activity, which elevates fatty acid synthesis and eventual triglyceride accumulation in hepatocytes (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: HMGCRs form spatial assemblies at yeast ER-lysosome contact sites.
source: Our work provides evidence that HMGCRs form similar spatial assemblies at yeast ER-lysosome contact sites, implicating a role for inter-organelle junctions in the spatial coordination of metabolically-induced enzymatic assembly formation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the BN-PAGE and localization data.

claim: Inter-organelle junctions play a role in the spatial coordination of metabolically-induced enzymatic assembly formation.
source: Our work provides evidence that HMGCRs form similar spatial assemblies at yeast ER-lysosome contact sites, implicating a role for inter-organelle junctions in the spatial coordination of metabolically-induced enzymatic assembly formation.
evidence: This is a broader implication inferred from the findings about HMGCR assemblies at the NVJ.
